title: Development Economics Adventure 1: HDI & Capabilities
welcome_lead: Today you'll measure development beyond GDP with the HDI and the capabilities approach.
meta_desc: Economics Development: Human Development Index and Sen's capabilities approach.
final_note: You computed an HDI score and explored Sen's capabilities approach.

concepts.def: What people actually do or are

walkthroughs.body_html:
GDP per capita misses inequality, services, leisure and environment.

The HDI (UNDP, 1990; Mahbub ul Haq & Sen) combines three dimensions equally:

1. Health — life expectancy at birth.
2. Education — mean and expected years of schooling.
3. Income — GNI per capita (PPP $).

Each is normalised and averaged geometrically.

Amartya Sen (1985, 1999): development is the expansion of capabilities — the freedoms a person has to lead a life they value.

Capabilities → Functionings (what one actually does/is).

Income enables, but does not define, capability. A wheelchair user needs more income to achieve the same mobility — the 'conversion factor'.

Strengths: multidimensional, comparable, drives policy debate.

Limits: equal weights are arbitrary, ignores inequality (IHDI corrects), gender (GII), sustainability (PHDI), political freedoms.

Composite indices simplify but can hide trade-offs.

mcqs.q: Sen's term for real freedoms people enjoy:
Is a trade deficit necessarily bad?
options: Comparative advantage means richer countries should help poorer ones.
A trade deficit always means a country is losing wealth and failing economically.
A trade deficit means a country has no factories.
Not necessarily — it can reflect strong domestic demand, attractive investment opportunities, or borrowing to fund growth. Context matters more than the headline figure.

mcqs.q: What is the predicted effect of a binding price ceiling like rent control?
options: Shortage in the market — quantity demanded exceeds quantity supplied at the controlled price, leading to queues, black markets and reduced quality.
Price ceilings make goods cheaper for everyone with no downsides.
Comparative advantage means richer countries should help poorer ones.
Price ceilings only affect the rich.

mcqs.q: What is the principle of comparative advantage?
options: A trade deficit means a country has no factories.
Countries should specialise in producing goods with lower opportunity cost relative to others — even a country worse at everything still has a comparative advantage in something.
A country should produce whatever it can make best.
Comparative advantage means richer countries should help poorer ones.
